subject: saving with other people in a group to afford something one person could not
citation: Matuku & Kaseke (2014), 'The role of stokvels in improving people's lives: Orange Farm, Johannesburg', Social Work/Maatskaplike Werk

claims.text: A stokvel works because it separates grocery money from other claims on irregular income, creating a disciplined buffer that smooths consumption across the year.
objections: Will the groceries I get match the money I put in?

claims.text: A burial society works because witnessing neighbours' funeral hardship turns shared vulnerability into a pooled response of equipment, labour and presence.
A rotating savings scheme works because small regular contributions are locked away from daily temptation, converting them into a lump sum that buys assets or pays large bills.
objections: Can I trust these people with my contributions?

claims.text: A stokvel works as a credit source because lending is confined mainly to a trusted circle, occasionally extending to trusted outsiders, where lender and borrower know each other's circumstances and social ties enforce repayment.
objections: Do I know where the borrowers live?

claims.text: A stokvel spreads because visible uniforms and personal networks signal an accessible, socially endorsed institution with clear entry rules.
objections: How do I join and what does it cost to enter?
